description: We’re a team of driven students who turn ideas into real impact. Winners of the AI Hackathon 2026, organized with Egypt’s Ministry of Communications and Information Technology and Orange Digital Center, we combine AI expertise, creativity, and teamwork to build solutions that matter. Every member brings a unique strength, and we push each other to learn, innovate, and deliver with quality. Proven under pressure, we’re ready for the next challenge.
summary: We developed a web app that lets anyone pick a NASA Earth variable and a region, plots its time series, and tests whether the trend is significant. It meets the challenge by covering variable selection, regional data, visualization, rate of change and significance tests (Mann-Kendall, regression, confidence intervals). It matters because it makes NASA data understandable for students and the public.
details:
What it does and how it works: NASA-EARTH Detective Trend is a free website that lets anyone play data detective with real NASA data. You pick a variable, like temperature, rainfall or wind, then choose a place on the map and a time period from 1981 to today. The app pulls the data from NASA’s POWER API, draws the time series, and tells you whether the change is real or just noise, using linear regression, the Mann-Kendall test, Sen’s slope and confidence intervals. It also removes the seasonal ups and downs so the long-term trend is easier to spot, and it explains the result in plain language.

Why we built it: NASA data is powerful, but most people can’t use it. There are hundreds of variables, trends can go in opposite directions in different regions, and judging significance takes statistics knowledge. We wanted a student or a curious person with no coding background to get a clear answer in a few clicks.

Benefits and intended impact: The app makes NASA Earth data understandable for students, teachers and the public. It is free, needs no installation, and works on any device. In the long run, we hope it helps people think more with evidence about farming, energy, health and climate.

Tools and technologies: We built it with HTML, CSS and JavaScript, including our own statistics engine. Plotly draws the charts, Leaflet runs the maps, Three.js powers the 3D globe, and ExcelJS handles the Excel export. The data comes from the NASA POWER API, and the site is hosted for free on GitHub Pages. No special hardware is needed, since it runs in any browser.

What makes it creative: We wanted it to feel like exploring, not just analyzing. You can spin a 3D Earth, step inside a 360° view of a place, try ready-made demos, check a glossary, revisit your past searches, and export everything to Excel with the chart included.

Factors we considered: We thought carefully about who would use it, so we kept the steps simple and the results in plain language. We chose tests that work for messy real-world data and removed seasonal cycles so they don’t hide real trends. We were also upfront about the limits: the data has a 0.5° resolution, longer periods give more reliable trends, and results are for learning and exploring, not a replacement for peer-reviewed research.
